An image is a recipe packed with application files. A container is a running copy of that recipe. A volume is a storage box kept outside that disposable running copy.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Prepare your computer

Install Docker Desktop with Linux containers enabled and the .NET10 SDK. For the full SQL Server stack use supported x64 hardware with enough memory for SQL Server. WPF does not run in the Linux ASP.NET image. Accept applicable vendor licences yourself during installation. Run docker version and docker compose version in a terminal; start Docker Desktop if the engine cannot be reached.

Compare the boundaries

  • A virtual machine has its own guest operating-system kernel. Containers usually share the host kernel while isolating processes, filesystems and networking. On Windows/macOS, Docker Desktop uses a Linux environment for Linux containers.
  • An image is layered and read-only. A container adds a writable layer and a process. Deleting the container discards that layer, not a separately kept named volume.
  • A registry stores images. A repository groups related images; a tag identifies a labelled version. A tag can move, while a digest identifies particular content.
  • A container is not a guarantee of perfect security. Run least-privileged processes, limit exposed ports, update images and avoid mounting the Docker socket into ordinary applications.

First commands

docker version
docker compose version
docker image ls
docker ps -a

Expected: client/server version details, Compose version, local images and containers. Exact versions/IDs differ. Cannot connect to daemon means Docker Desktop or the engine is not ready.

Try it yourself

Does rebuilding an image automatically replace a running container?

Worked answer

No. Create/recreate the container from the new image, for example docker compose up --build -d.

Can a Windows WPF window run in this Linux API container?

Worked answer

No. WPF is Windows desktop technology. Containerise the server/API parts using supported images.
